notes.h: Factors that shape food choices: culture, religion, eating patterns and sensory aspects
notes.b: Nobody picks food in a vacuum. A food choice results from several pressures acting together, and each one can be named and explained on its own, with an example.
points: Culture: the shared customs and traditions of a group decide which foods are normal, acceptable or celebratory, and certain foods are linked with a particular country, tradition or festival.
Travel, television and immigration spread foods from one culture to another, so people often eat dishes that did not belong to their own country's tradition.
Religion: some faiths restrict foods, so a person's beliefs can rule certain foods out. Jews and Muslims do not eat pork, and some Hindus follow a vegetarian diet.
Eating patterns: the number and timing of meals, snacking, eating out and whether the family eats together all shape what is bought and eaten.
Irregular family routines change what is bought and cooked, because people who eat at different times tend to rely on quick foods rather than a shared cooked meal.
Sensory aspects: taste, smell, appearance, texture and temperature decide whether a food is accepted, and unfamiliar flavours are often refused at first.
Likes and dislikes, the way food is presented and early exposure to fatty, salty and sugary food shape preferences, which is why children who grow up on these foods often keep choosing them.
notes.tip: Culture and religion are separate factors. If a question asks for two factors, give them as two separate answers. Say 'some Hindus' and 'Jews and Muslims do not eat pork', never that every follower of a faith avoids a food. Do not mix up eating patterns (when and how often) with availability (what can be bought).

notes.h: Factors that shape food choices: nutrition, health, availability, finance and marketing
notes.b: The remaining factors are about knowledge, the body, the shops and the money in a person's pocket. Name each factor, then explain it with an example in a sentence.
points: Nutritional awareness: knowledge of healthy eating guidelines and of food labels steers people towards lower-fat, lower-sugar and higher-fibre products, while low awareness leads to poorer choices.
Health status: allergies and intolerances, coeliac disease, diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure and weight management limit or direct what a person can safely eat.
Because of these conditions people buy foods such as lactose-free, gluten-free, low-cholesterol and allergy-safe products.
Availability: seasonal produce, the range stocked by local shops, the distance to a supermarket, access to a car and the foods sold in a school canteen or vending machine determine what is on offer.
Finance: income sets the budget. People with more money buy expensive foods more often, eat out and meet foreign foods on holidays.
People on low incomes tend to buy cheaper and more processed foods, own brands, special offers and inexpensive protein such as pulses, eggs and tinned fish.

Marketing and advertising: packaging, brand image, special offers, shelf placement, endorsements by celebrities or influencers and social media encourage purchases, and advertising to children and teenagers is especially influential.
notes.tip: Nutritional awareness is about knowledge, while health status is about a condition that forces a choice. Availability is what can be bought, finance is what can be afforded. Keep each in its own answer. For health status, name the condition and the food bought as a result.

notes.b: Two further influences are examined even though they are not separate syllabus factors. They fit under eating patterns, availability, nutritional awareness and culture.
points: Convenience and lifestyle: lack of time or cooking skill increases the use of ready meals and takeaways, so busy households choose food that is quick to prepare.
Eating food away from home covers restaurants, cafés, hotels, takeaways, delicatessens and pub food. More people do it because they have more money and choice, less time and less cooking skill.
Health and wellbeing: people choose foods for health reasons, such as less fat, salt and sugar and more fibre, which is an example of nutritional awareness at work.

Responsible living: people also choose foods for ethical and environmental reasons, such as organic, Fairtrade, local and seasonal foods, less food waste, animal welfare and sustainability. These choices reflect personal values and culture.
notes.tip: A question on health and responsible living wants both sides: choosing food for your own health, and choosing it for ethical and environmental reasons. A question on eating food away from home wants its meaning and why more people do it: more money and choice, less time and lack of cooking skill.

notes.h: Changes in Irish eating patterns since the early twentieth century
notes.b: Irish eating habits have changed a great deal over the last century. These changes describe the whole population over time, so they are trends such as more convenience food and less home cooking.
points: Potatoes and bread have been partly replaced by pasta, rice and a wider range of breads, because a wider food range has become available.
Convenience, ready-meal and processed foods have become more common, bringing more salt, sugar, saturated fat and additives and less fibre into the diet.
Eating out, takeaways and fast food have increased, as has eating on the go. This includes eating food away from home in restaurants, cafés, hotels, takeaways, delicatessens and pubs.
Meals have become more irregular: family members often eat at different times, so the main meal, now in the evening, is less often eaten together.
Foreign holidays, television, the internet, travel, immigration and food bloggers have introduced new cuisines and ingredients to Irish diets, such as ethnic cuisines.
Microwaving, stir-frying and barbecuing are now common cooking methods in Irish homes, and people also have less time for cooking at home.
Greater health and nutritional awareness has encouraged more fruit, vegetables, wholegrain, organic, functional and fortified foods.
Intermittent fasting and plant-based eating are recent trends, reflecting people's interest in health.
notes.tip: Questions on changes since the early twentieth century want trends, such as more convenience food and less home cooking, not a list of factors. Give each change with a short explanation of its effect, for example convenience food bringing more salt, sugar and saturated fat.

notes.b: Very young children do not choose for themselves. Parents decide, and they weigh up several things.
points: Parents make most food choices for pre-school children, weighing nutrition and the food pyramid, cost, allergies and health, and the degree of processing.
They also consider a portion size suited to a small child, ease of handling, packaging and labelling, and family habits.
Young children often refuse new foods at first and may need to be offered a food many times before accepting it. This reluctance is called food neophobia.
Involving children in preparation and presenting food attractively encourages them to try new foods, because the food becomes familiar and appealing.
notes.tip: For pre-school children, name the considerations parents weigh (nutrition, cost, processing, allergies, portion size, labelling) rather than the children's own preferences, since the parents make the choices.

notes.b: Teenagers start to make their own food decisions, and the influences on them are different from those on young children.
points: Teenagers' choices are influenced by peer groups, advertising and social media, independence and a wish to eat out.
They have money of their own from pocket money or part-time work, which gives them the buying power to choose for themselves.
Body image, convenience and busy lives also play a part in what teenagers choose.
Many teenagers prefer fatty, salty and sugary foods, which they have often been exposed to since early childhood.
A teenager may choose a vegetarian diet for cultural, religious, moral or ethical reasons such as animal welfare, or for health, environmental, economic or family reasons, or because of peers.
Culture and religion affect young people through foods linked with cultures, religious restrictions, travel, television, immigration and multicultural influences.
notes.tip: A question on why some teenagers become vegetarian asks for separate reasons, each explained: culture, religion, moral or ethical views (animal welfare), health, environment, economic reasons and family or peers. Link answers about healthy eating to the factors that make it difficult for teenagers.

notes.b: Students in school or living away from home share many teenage influences, but time, money and facilities limit what they can choose.
points: Students in post-primary school choose according to personal preference, cost, nutritional awareness, advertising and peers.
Health status and allergies, and activity level, also affect their choices.
The range sold in the canteen or vending machines, and whether there are facilities to reheat food, decide what is practical.
Students living away or on a budget face the same factors, with limited time, money and cooking skill, so they tend to choose quick, cheap foods.

notes.h: Answering questions on food choice data
notes.b: Higher Level exams give a table or chart and ask you to comment on it. A clear routine earns the marks.
points: Describe the overall trend first, then support it with specific figures read from the data.
Compare two groups, such as parents and children or boys and girls, by stating which group is higher and by how much.
Suggest reasons for differences by drawing on the factors that shape food choices, because the data only shows what people choose, not why.

Relate the results to healthy eating guidelines, saying whether consumption meets them or falls short, for example whether five or more portions of fruit and vegetables a day (Department of Health Food Pyramid) are being reached.
Comment on what the results mean for planning meals or for health and health education.
notes.tip: Data parts at Higher Level expect the trend, a comparison, reasons from the factor list and a link to the guidelines. Use the figures printed in the question, not figures from memory.

notes.b: These are practical contexts that help you practise applying the factors.
points: Comparing meal patterns between countries, such as when the main meal is eaten and how many meals are normal.
A theme day or week on the foods of a culture or period, such as a traditional Irish breakfast.

keyTerms.definition: The decision to buy and eat a particular food, shaped by personal, social and economic factors.
The shared customs, beliefs and traditions of a group that determine which foods are regarded as normal, acceptable or special.
The taste, smell, appearance, texture and temperature of food, which affect whether it is enjoyed and accepted.
Knowledge of healthy eating guidance and food composition that guides a person's choice of foods.
Food that is ready to eat or needs little preparation, such as ready meals and pre-cut vegetables.
Food that has been changed from its natural state by methods such as canning, freezing, curing or adding ingredients.
A reluctance to try new or unfamiliar foods, most common in young children.
The effect of friends and classmates on what a young person chooses to eat.

factCards.term: Eight factors that influence food choices
factCards.definition: Culture, eating patterns, sensory aspects, nutritional awareness, health status, availability, finance, and marketing and advertising.

factCards.term: Three ways culture affects food choices
factCards.definition: Certain foods are associated with particular cultures; religious rules exclude or require certain foods; immigration and travel bring new foods into the diet.

factCards.term: Three changes in Irish eating habits since the early twentieth century
factCards.definition: More convenience and processed food; more eating out and fast food; less time for cooking and more irregular meals.

factCards.term: Two reasons teenagers find it hard to eat a healthy diet
factCards.definition: Convenience and eating on the go; cheap, heavily advertised processed food.

factCards.term: Two ways money affects food choices
factCards.definition: Higher income allows more frequent eating out and expensive foods; lower income leads to cheaper options, own-brand foods and fewer luxury items.

factCards.term: Three factors parents consider for pre-school children
factCards.definition: Nutrition, health and allergies; cost and degree of processing; portion size suited to a small child.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which religious beliefs can influence a family's food choices.
questions.model: Religious rules exclude certain foods, for example Jews and Muslims do not eat pork, so these foods are avoided at home and when eating out. Some Hindus follow a vegetarian diet, so meals are built around pulses, dairy, vegetables and grains. Fasting periods and religious festivals also change meal times and the foods served. Any two ways, each with a name and an explanation, earn 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how advertising and marketing, together with the range of food available locally, can influence the food choices of teenagers.
questions.model: Advertising and marketing: television, social media and influencers promote sugary drinks, fast food and snacks, often through celebrities. Bright packaging and cartoon characters appeal to young people. Special offers, bundle deals and placement at checkouts encourage impulse buying. Local availability: a town with many takeaways and convenience stores offers fewer fresh options, and vending machines in schools can limit healthy choices. A shop stocking fresh fruit, vegetables and wholegrain bread makes healthy choices easier. Peer and social factors: teenagers copy friends' eating habits and eat together in groups where fast food is popular. Evaluation: teenagers with good nutritional awareness can resist marketing, but family influence and cost still limit what they can choose.
